added_lemmas.statement:
For every \(\theta\in\Theta_{\mathrm{pop}}\) and every integer \(k\geq2\),
\[
 m_k-\beta c_k=\alpha^{k-1}\gamma u_k\in A,
 \qquad Q_Am_k=\beta Q_Ac_k.
\]
These identities require only finite moments through order \(k\), source independence, and the population-plane restriction; they do not require a moment generating function.
added_lemmas.proof_tex:
Fix \(\theta\in\Theta_{\mathrm{pop}}\) and an integer \(k\geq2\).  All moments appearing below are finite by the all-absolute-moments condition in the definition of \(\Theta_{\mathrm{pop}}\).  For random variables \(X_1,\ldots,X_k\) with finite absolute moments through order \(k\), their joint cumulant is the finite moment--cumulant polynomial
\[
 \kappa_k(X_1,\ldots,X_k)
 =\sum_{\pi\in\mathfrak P_k}(|\pi|-1)!(-1)^{|\pi|-1}
   \prod_{D\in\pi}\mathbb E\!\left[\prod_{j\in D}X_j\right],             \tag{1}
\]
where \(\mathfrak P_k\) is the set of partitions of \(\{1,\ldots,k\}\).  Formula (1) is multilinear because, after each product is expanded, every argument occurs exactly once in every summand.  It also shows that a cumulant involving variables from two independent source families is zero.  To verify the latter without an analytic moment-generating function, introduce the finite formal moment series in indeterminates \(t_1,\ldots,t_k\), retain only monomials in which every exponent is at most one, and expand the formal logarithm \(\log(1+z)=\sum_{j=1}^k(-1)^{j-1}z^j/j\).  The coefficient of \(t_1\cdots t_k\) is exactly (1).  Independence factors the formal moment series into one factor for each independent source family, so its formal logarithm is a sum of terms involving only one family; hence every mixed coefficient vanishes.  This argument uses only the finitely many moments in (1).

Define the proof-local treatment-source contrast
\[
 v_k=\bigl(\kappa_k(\epsilon_{t,e})-
                 \kappa_k(\epsilon_{t,0})\bigr)_{e=1}^{E-1}.
\]
The structural equations give
\[
 T_e=\alpha\epsilon_{u,e}+\epsilon_{t,e},
 \qquad
 Y_e=(\alpha\beta+\gamma)\epsilon_{u,e}
       +\beta\epsilon_{t,e}+\epsilon_y.                                  \tag{2}
\]
By multilinearity of (1), mutual independence of the three sources, and vanishing of mixed-source cumulants,
\[
 \kappa_k(T_e)=\alpha^k\kappa_k(\epsilon_{u,e})
                  +\kappa_k(\epsilon_{t,e}),                              \tag{3}
\]
and, because \(k\geq2\),
\[
 \kappa_k(Y_e,T_e,\ldots,T_e)
 =(alpha\beta+\gamma)\alpha^{k-1}\kappa_k(\epsilon_{u,e})
   +\beta\kappa_k(\epsilon_{t,e}).                                       \tag{4}
\]
The invariant outcome source contributes nothing to (4): any term selecting \(\epsilon_y\) in the first argument and a treatment source in a remaining argument is a mixed cumulant of independent families.

Subtracting the baseline-environment versions of (3)--(4) and using the definitions of \(u_k,c_k,m_k\) yields
\[
 c_k=\alpha^ku_k+v_k,                                                       \tag{5}
\]
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 m_k
 &=(\alpha\beta+\gamma)\alpha^{k-1}u_k+\beta v_k\\
 &=\beta(\alpha^ku_k+v_k)+\alpha^{k-1}\gamma u_k
  =\beta c_k+\alpha^{k-1}\gamma u_k.                                     \tag{6}
 \end{aligned}
\]
The population-plane restriction gives \(u_k\in A\), so (6) proves \(m_k-\beta c_k\in A\).  Since \(\operatorname{rank}(C)=d\), the matrix \(C^\top C\) is invertible and the declared operator \(Q_A\) is the orthogonal projector onto \(A^\perp\).  Applying it to (6) gives \(Q_Am_k=\beta Q_Ac_k\), as required.

added_lemmas.statement: The bounded calibrated class is a subclass of the population flag class: \(\Theta\subseteq\Theta_{\mathrm{pop}}\).
added_lemmas.proof_tex: Let \(\theta\in\Theta\).  The ambient-class definition supplies the same three structural equations as the population-class definition.  Its source-independence member property supplies mutual independence within every environment, and its all-absolute-moments member property supplies finite absolute moments of every positive integer order.  Its calibration-rank property gives \(\operatorname{rank}(C)=d\), and its latent-profile-plane property gives \(u_k\in A\) for every integer \(k\geq2\).  These are precisely the membership requirements of \(\Theta_{\mathrm{pop}}\); the remaining coefficient, moment-envelope, order-cap, and singular-gap restrictions defining \(\Theta\) only make the class smaller.  Thus \(\theta\in\Theta_{\mathrm{pop}}\), proving \(\Theta\subseteq\Theta_{\mathrm{pop}}\).

The causal target is the structural coefficient \(\beta\), not the right-hand side of (1).  Indeed, under the intervention setting treatment to \(t\), while leaving the exogenous variables fixed, the structural equation gives
\[
 Y_e(t)=\beta t+\gamma U_e+\epsilon_y,
 \qquad Y_e(t+1)-Y_e(t)=\beta.                                             \tag{2}
\]
We now prove that the observable quotient equals this target under the stated population restrictions.

Let \(\theta\in\Theta_{\mathrm{pop}}\), and suppose \(Q_Ac_k\neq0\) for some integer \(k\geq2\).  The population cumulant-cancellation lemma gives
\[
 Q_Am_k=\beta Q_Ac_k.                                                       \tag{3}
\]
Taking the Euclidean inner product of (3) with \(Q_Ac_k\) gives
\[
 \langle Q_Ac_k,Q_Am_k\rangle
 =\beta\lVert Q_Ac_k\rVert_2^2.                                          \tag{4}
\]
The assumed nonzero flag makes the denominator in (4) strictly positive, so division proves (1).

Every object on the right of (1) is determined by the observed laws.  The required moments exist in \(\Theta_{\mathrm{pop}}\), so \(P_e\) determines \(c_k\) and \(m_k\).  It also determines \(C=[c_2\mid\cdots\mid c_{d+1}]\).  The population rank condition gives \(\operatorname{rank}(C)=d\), hence \(C^\top C\) is invertible and \(P=(P_e:e\in\mathcal E)\) determines \(Q_A=I-C(C^\top C)^{-1}C^\top\).  Now let \(\widetilde\theta\in\Theta_{\mathrm{pop}}\) have the same observed laws as \(\theta\).  It has the same \(c_k,m_k,C,Q_A\), and therefore the same \(r^\star\).  If \(r^\star<\infty\), apply (1) at \(k=r^\star\) to both representations to obtain
\[
 \widetilde\beta
 =\frac{\langle Q_Ac_{r^\star},Q_Am_{r^\star}\rangle}
        {\lVert Q_Ac_{r^\star}\rVert_2^2}
 =\beta.                                                                   \tag{5}
\]
No order cap was used, so (5) includes \(r^\star>R_{\max}\).  This proves point identification relative to the broad population class.

We next specialize to \(\mathcal D_\rho\).  The ambient-subclass lemma gives \(\Theta\subseteq\Theta_{\mathrm{pop}}\), hence every member of \(\mathcal B\) with finite breakout is identified by (5).  Equivalently, if a second member of \(\mathcal D_\rho\) has the same observed laws, then it has the same finite \(r^\star\), cannot belong to the no-breakout branch, and (5) gives the same effect.

Let now \(\theta\in\mathcal N_\rho\).  The treatment-loading bound in \(\Theta_\rho^\circ\) gives \(|\alpha|\geq a_0+\rho>0\), so the proof-local quantity \(q=\gamma/\alpha\) is well defined.  Put
\[
 V_e=\alpha\epsilon_{u,e},\qquad W_e=\epsilon_{t,e}.
\]
The observed variables under \(\theta\) are
\[
 T_e=V_e+W_e,
 \qquad
 Y_e=(\beta+q)V_e+\beta W_e+\epsilon_y.                                   \tag{6}
\]
Under \(S\theta\), the latent and treatment sources are respectively \(W_e\) and \(V_e\), while the coefficients are \(1,\beta+q,-q\).  Therefore
\[
 T_e'=W_e+V_e,
 \qquad
 Y_e'=(\beta+q)(W_e+V_e)-qW_e+\epsilon_y
     =(\beta+q)V_e+\beta W_e+\epsilon_y.                                  \tag{7}
\]
Equations (6)--(7) prove equality of the complete observed laws in every environment, not merely equality of selected moments.

By definition of \(\mathcal N_\rho\), both \(\theta\) and \(S\theta\) lie in \(\Theta_\rho^\circ\), and both have infinite breakout.  To check that the second representation itself belongs to \(\mathcal N_\rho\), compute
\[
 S^2\theta
 =\left(1,\beta,q,
   \{\alpha\epsilon_{u,e},\epsilon_{t,e}\}_{e\in\mathcal E},\epsilon_y\right).       \tag{8}
\]
The loading value one is interior because it is already the loading of \(S\theta\); the effect \(\beta\) and confounding ratio \(q\) satisfy the interior bounds because \(\theta\) does.  The two source families in (8) are exactly the two source families of \(S\theta\) in the opposite structural roles, so their centering, independence, all-order moment property, and \((2R_{\max}+\delta)\)-moment bounds follow from \(S\theta\in\Theta_\rho^\circ\).  Its latent contrast is \(\alpha^ku_k\in A\) at order \(k\), and (6)--(7) show that its observed \(C\), calibration gap, and infinite breakout are unchanged.  Hence \(S^2\theta\in\Theta_\rho^\circ\) with infinite breakout.  Thus \(S\theta\in\mathcal N_\rho\subseteq\mathcal D_\rho\).

Finally, the two effects differ by \(q=\gamma/\alpha\), and the confounding bound gives \(|q|\geq q_0>0\).  Since the same observed laws correspond to two distinct values of the causal target within \(\mathcal D_\rho\), no observed-law functional identifies \(\beta\) at any member of \(\mathcal N_\rho\).  Combining this witness with finite-breakout identification proves the asserted if-and-only-if frontier on \(\mathcal D_\rho\).
added_lemmas.justification: This theorem separates unrestricted-order population identification from the bounded legal-swap domain and gives the explicit observed-law map in both settings.
added_lemmas.gap: The result is for a new calibrated low-rank multi-environment submodel; it does not assert identification for arbitrary simultaneous shifts in the class studied by Kivva et al.
added_lemmas.consumer: For a selected Sachs-panel edge, a finite environmental flag returns the direct-effect functional even above the inference order cap, while the bounded no-flag branch reports exact source-label ambiguity.

added_lemmas.statement:
Let \(d=1\), \(E=3\), and \(r\in\{3,\ldots,R_{\max}\}\).  Put \(x_0=0,x_1=1,x_2=2\) and \(y_0=0,y_1=2,y_2=-1\), and define
\[
 a=(x_1-x_0,x_2-x_0)^\top=(1,2)^\top,
 \qquad b=(y_1-y_0,y_2-y_0)^\top=(2,-1)^\top.
\]
For positive \(\eta,\zeta,\varepsilon\), there are centered compound-Poisson latent and treatment sources with cumulant-shift profiles
\[
 u_k=\eta a,
 \qquad
 w_k:=\bigl(\kappa_k(\epsilon_{t,e})-
                  \kappa_k(\epsilon_{t,0})\bigr)_{e=1}^2
      =\zeta a+\varepsilon\Delta_{r,k}b,
 \quad
 \Delta_{r,k}=\sum_{j=0}^r(-1)^{r-j}{r\choose j}j^k,                       \tag{1}
\]
where \(\Delta_{r,k}=0\) for \(k<r\) and \(\Delta_{r,r}=r!\).  Suppose the positive Poisson baselines are chosen so that every intensity in the construction is positive, and choose \(q>0\), an invariant centered Gaussian outcome source, and model bounds so that
\[
 a_0+\rho<1<a_1-\rho,quad
 q_0+\rho\leq q\leq q_1-\rho,quad
 q/2\leq B-\rho,quad
 \eta+\zeta\geq\kappa_0+\rho,                                             \tag{2}
\]
and the source \((2R_{\max}+\delta)\)-moments are at most \(M-\rho\).  With \(\alpha=1\), \(\beta=-q/2\), and \(\gamma=q\), the resulting parameter has \(A=\operatorname{span}(a)\), \(r^\star=r\), and is jointly identified.  Both source laws change between every pair of environments.  Nevertheless, on each of the three two-environment restrictions the scalar calibration contrast \(c_2^{ef}\) is nonzero and the legal source swap gives an observationally equivalent no-breakout representation with effect \(q/2\).  Jointly, the swapped latent profile at order \(r\) is not in \(A\), so that swapped representation is excluded by the maintained population-plane restriction.
added_lemmas.proof_tex:
For \(e\in\{0,1,2\}\), let
\[
 N^u_e\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(L_u+\eta x_e),
 \qquad
 \epsilon_{u,e}=N^u_e-(L_u+\eta x_e),                                    \tag{3}
\]
where \(L_u>0\).  Independently, for \(j=1,\ldots,r\), let
\[
 N^t_{e,j}\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda_{e,j}^t),
 \quad
 \lambda_{e,j}^t
 =L_j+\zeta x_e\mathbf 1\{j=1\}
   +\varepsilon y_e(-1)^{r-j}{r\choose j},                               \tag{4}
\]
and set
\[
 \epsilon_{t,e}=\sum_{j=1}^r j\bigl(N^t_{e,j}-\lambda_{e,j}^t\bigr).      \tag{5}
\]
Choose
\[
 L_j>\max_{e\in\{0,1,2\}}
 \left|\zeta x_e\mathbf 1\{j=1\}
   +\varepsilon y_e(-1)^{r-j}{r\choose j}\right|                         \tag{6}
\]
for every \(j\); then all intensities in (4) are strictly positive.  Take all Poisson counts mutually independent and take \(\epsilon_y\) to be an independent centered Gaussian variable.  Compensating each count proves centering.  Finite compound-Poisson sums and the Gaussian source have moment generating functions finite on the real line, hence in particular have every finite absolute moment.  The explicit feasibility premise on the \((2R_{\max}+\delta)\)-moments and (2) puts the construction, and each source-swapped pairwise restriction, inside the required bounded interiors.

For a compensated Poisson variable with jump size \(j\) and intensity \(\lambda\), every cumulant of order \(k\geq2\) is \(\lambda j^k\).  Thus (3) gives
\[
 u_k=\eta(x_1-x_0,x_2-x_0)^\top=\eta a.                                  \tag{7}
\]
Equations (4)--(5) give
\[
 w_k=\zeta a+\varepsilon b
       \sum_{j=0}^r(-1)^{r-j}{r\choose j}j^k.                             \tag{8}
\]
The sum in (8) is the \(r\)-th forward difference at zero of the polynomial \(z\mapsto z^k\).  An \(r\)-th forward difference annihilates every polynomial of degree below \(r\), while the \(r\)-th difference of \(z^r\) is the constant \(r!\).  Therefore
\[
 \Delta_{r,k}=0\quad(k<r),
 \qquad \Delta_{r,r}=r!.                                                  \tag{9}
\]

Set \(\alpha=1\), \(\beta=-q/2\), and \(\gamma=q\).  By independence and cumulant additivity, the observed treatment contrasts are
\[
 c_k=u_k+w_k=(\eta+\zeta)a+\varepsilon\Delta_{r,k}b.                      \tag{10}
\]
Since \(r\geq3\), (9) gives \(\Delta_{r,2}=0\).  Hence
\[
 C=[c_2]=[(\eta+\zeta)a],
 \qquad A=\operatorname{span}(a),
 \qquad \sigma_1(C)=(\eta+\zeta)\|a\|_2\geq\kappa_0+\rho.             \tag{11}
\]
The latent profiles (7) lie in \(A\) at every order.  Equations (9)--(10) show \(Q_Ac_k=0\) for \(k<r\).  Because
\[
 \langle a,b\rangle=1\cdot2+2\cdot(-1)=0,
 \qquad b\neq0,                                                           \tag{12}
\]
we have
\[
 Q_Ac_r=\varepsilon r!b\neq0.                                             \tag{13}
\]
Thus \(r^\star=r\), and the population identification theorem identifies the original effect jointly by its quotient at order \(r\).

We next check the pairwise claim.  For distinct \(e,f\in\{0,1,2\}\), the latent variance contrast is \(\eta(x_e-x_f)\), which is nonzero because the three \(x_e\)'s are distinct.  By (8)--(9), the treatment-source variance contrast is \(\zeta(x_e-x_f)\), also nonzero.  Hence both source laws change in every environment pair.  The observed scalar calibration contrast for that pair is
\[
 c_2^{ef}=(\eta+\zeta)(x_e-x_f)\neq0.                                    \tag{14}
\]
In a two-environment restriction with \(d=1\), the nonzero scalar (14) spans the entire one-dimensional contrast space.  Its orthogonal projector is therefore zero, so every cumulant flag vanishes in both source orderings.  The inequalities in (2), the moment premise, and positivity (6) make the swap legal in the pairwise bounded class.  Directly, the original representation is
\[
 T_e=\epsilon_{u,e}+\epsilon_{t,e},
 \qquad
 Y_e=\frac q2\epsilon_{u,e}-\frac q2\epsilon_{t,e}+\epsilon_y,           \tag{15}
\]
whereas its source swap uses latent source \(\epsilon_{t,e}\), treatment source \(\epsilon_{u,e}\), and coefficients \((1,q/2,-q)\).  Substitution gives exactly the same two variables in (15), while the direct effect changes from \(-q/2\) to \(q/2\).  This proves legal unequal-effect no-breakout ambiguity separately for every pair.

Finally, the jointly swapped latent source is the original treatment source, whose order-\(r\) profile is
\[
 w_r=\zeta a+\varepsilon r!b.                                             \tag{16}
\]
By (12) and \(\varepsilon>0\), (16) is not in \(A=\operatorname{span}(a)\).  Thus the pairwise swaps cannot be assembled into an admissible joint representation: the joint swap violates the population-plane restriction.  Equations (13)--(16) establish the claimed pairwise ambiguity and joint rescue.
added_lemmas.justification: The construction certifies genuine joint rescue: every environment pair remains source-swap ambiguous even though the three-environment flag identifies the effect.
added_lemmas.gap: The nearest published two-environment obstruction does not provide a same-model three-environment witness whose pairwise swaps are legal but whose joint swap violates a calibrated latent plane.
added_lemmas.consumer: It explains why a perturbation panel can be informative jointly even when every pairwise protein-signaling comparison is structurally ambiguous.

added_lemmas.proof_tex:
Put \(s_0=2R_{\max}+\delta\).  The treatment-loading, confounding, effect, and source-moment bounds imply
\[
 |\gamma|=|\alpha|\,|\gamma/\alpha|\leq a_1q_1.
\]
Minkowski's inequality in \(L^{s_0}\), applied to the two structural equations, therefore gives a constant \(K_0<\infty\), depending only on the fixed envelopes, such that
\[
 \sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\max_{e\in\mathcal E}
 \mathbb E_\theta\left[|T_e|^{s_0}+|Y_e|^{s_0}\right]\leq K_0.           \tag{4}
\]
The ratio in the first display is well defined because \(|\alpha|\geq a_0>0\).

For \(k\leq R_{\max}\), the moment--cumulant polynomial (1) in the population cumulant-cancellation proof expresses every cumulant used here as a finite polynomial in moments of total degree at most \(k\).  If \(\pi=\{D_1,\ldots,D_s\}\) is a partition occurring in that polynomial, an unbiased estimator of its product of moments in environment \(e\) is
\[
 \frac1{(n_e)_s}\sum_{i_1,\ldots,i_s\ {
m distinct}}
 \prod_{a=1}^s\prod_{j\in D_a}X_{j,e,i_a}.                               \tag{5}
\]
Independence across observations proves unbiasedness term by term.  The square of a summand in (5) has total degree at most \(2k\leq2R_{\max}<s_0\), so (4), Lyapunov's inequality, and H\"older's inequality bound its second moment uniformly.  In the variance double sum, disjoint index tuples are independent, and only \(O(n_e^{2s-1})\) of the \(O(n_e^{2s})\) pairs overlap.  The admitted orders, partitions, and environments are finite, and balanced shares give \(n_e\geq\underline\pi n\).  Consequently, whenever all \(n_e\geq R_{\max}\),
\[
 \sup_{\theta\in\Theta}
 \mathbb E_\theta\left[
  \|\widehat c_k-c_k\|_2^2+\|\widehat m_k-m_k\|_2^2
 \right]\leq\frac{K_1}{n},
 \qquad 2\leq k\leq R_{\max}.                                           \tag{6}
\]
The same polynomial and (4) uniformly bound \(\|c_k\|_2\) and \(\|m_k\|_2\).

Let \(H=\widehat C-C\), and let \(\widehat A\) be the rank-\(d\) left singular subspace used to construct \(\widehat Q\).  If \(\|H\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq\kappa_0/2\) and \(x=Cy\) is a unit vector in \(A\), then \(\|y\|_2\leq\kappa_0^{-1}\) and
\[
 \operatorname{dist}(x,\widehat A)
 \leq\|Hy\|_2\leq\kappa_0^{-1}\|H\|_{\mathrm{op}}.                    \tag{7}
\]
The variational definition of singular values gives
\[
 \sigma_d(\widehat C)\geq\sigma_d(C)-\|H\|_{\mathrm{op}}
 \geq\kappa_0/2.                                                          \tag{8}
\]
Thus if \(z=\widehat Cy\) is a unit vector in \(\widehat A\), then \(\|y\|_2\leq2/\kappa_0\) and
\[
 \operatorname{dist}(z,A)\leq2\kappa_0^{-1}\|H\|_{\mathrm{op}}.         \tag{9}
\]
The two directed distances (7) and (9), applied to the orthogonal decompositions for two equal-dimensional subspaces, imply
\[
 \|\widehat Q-Q_A\|_{\mathrm{op}}
 \leq4\kappa_0^{-1}\|H\|_{\mathrm{op}}.                                \tag{10}
\]
On the complementary event the left side is at most two.  Equation (6) for the fixed \(d\) columns of \(H\), followed by Markov's inequality, therefore yields
\[
 \sup_{\theta\in\Theta}
 \mathbb E_\theta\|\widehat Q-Q_A\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2\leq\frac{K_2}{n}. \tag{11}
\]
This calculation never inverts an influence covariance and permits that covariance to be singular.

For \(|b|\leq B\), define the proof intermediates
\[
 g_k(b)=Q_A(m_k-bc_k),
 \qquad \widehat g_k(b)=\widehat Q(\widehat m_k-b\widehat c_k),
\]
and
\[
 \Delta_n=\max_{d+2\leq k\leq R_{\max}}
 \sup_{|b|\leq B}\|\widehat g_k(b)-g_k(b)\|_2.
\]
The exact decomposition
\[
 \widehat g_k(b)-g_k(b)
 =\widehat Q\{(\widehat m_k-m_k)-b(\widehat c_k-c_k)\}
  +(\widehat Q-Q_A)(m_k-bc_k)                                             \tag{12}
\]
and (6), (11), and the population cumulant bounds imply
\[
 \sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\mathbb E_\theta\Delta_n^2\leq\frac{K_3}{n}.    \tag{13}
\]
This is the required uniform same-sample generated-plane control, and it uses neither \(r\), \(\lambda_n\), nor a nonzero flag.

The bounded cumulant-cancellation lemma applies to every \(\theta\in\Theta\), not only to \(\mathcal D_\rho\), and gives
\[
 g_k(b)=(\beta-b)Q_Ac_k,
 \qquad g_k(\beta)=0.                                                      \tag{14}
\]
If \(\theta\in\mathcal M_r(\lambda_n)\), optimality of the estimator and (12)--(14) yield
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 |\widehat\beta-\beta|\,\|Q_Ac_r\|_2
 &=\|g_r(\widehat\beta)\|_2\\
 &\leq\|\widehat g_r(\widehat\beta)\|_2+\Delta_n\\
 &\leq\max_k\|\widehat g_k(\widehat\beta)\|_2+\Delta_n\\
 &\leq\max_k\|\widehat g_k(\beta)\|_2+\Delta_n
 \leq2\Delta_n.                                                          \tag{15}
 \end{aligned}
\]
The minimizer exists because the objective is continuous on the compact interval \([-B,B]\).  Since the shell gives \(\|Q_Ac_r\|_2\geq\lambda_n\), and both effects lie in \([-B,B]\), (13)--(15) prove (1), after changing the constant.

Choose \(t_{\alpha_0}\) so that
\[
 t_{\alpha_0}^2\geq K_3/\alpha_0.                                        \tag{16}
\]
Let \(\mathcal R_n\) be the raw norm-sublevel set in the definition of \(\mathcal C_n\).  By (14), on \(\{\Delta_n\leq t_{\alpha_0}/\sqrt n\}\) the true \(\beta\) belongs to \(\mathcal R_n\).  On this event the raw set is nonempty, so its empty-set fallback is irrelevant.  Markov's inequality, (13), and (16) give
\[
 \inf_{\theta\in\Theta}
 \Pr_\theta\{\beta\in\mathcal C_n\}\geq1-\alpha_0.                    \tag{17}
\]
Thus the conservative coverage is valid on the entire bounded ambient class, including no-breakout parameters.  The prescribed small-sample set \([-B,B]\) covers identically.

Each constraint defining \(\mathcal R_n\) is a convex sublevel set of the norm of an affine function of the scalar \(b\), so their intersection with \([-B,B]\) is an interval.  If \(b,b'\in\mathcal R_n\), then on the shell, (12)--(14) give
\[
 |b-b'|\lambda_n
 \leq\|g_r(b)-g_r(b')\|_2
 \leq2\left(\frac{t_{\alpha_0}}{\sqrt n}+\Delta_n\right).               \tag{18}
\]
If \(\mathcal R_n\) is empty, the fallback is a singleton and has length zero.  The box bound \(2B\), (13), (18), and Cauchy--Schwarz prove (3).  The true \(r\) appears only in the analysis; both procedures maximize over all admitted orders.

Balanced shares imply that some \(n_e<R_{\max}\) only when \(n<R_{\max}/\underline\pi\).  The deterministic error and length bounds \(4B^2\) and \(2B\), together with the uniform cumulant bound \(\|Q_Ac_k\|_2\leq\Lambda\), allow enlargement of the constants in (1) and (3) to cover these finitely many sample sizes whenever the shell is nonempty.

We now construct one compatible bounded experiment giving both lower bounds, common to all admitted \(r\).  Put
\[
 J=[19/10,23/10],
 \qquad \Sigma=\begin{pmatrix}2&5\\5&14\end{pmatrix},
\]
and, for \(b\in J\), define
\[
 f_b=\frac{5-2b}{3-b},\qquad
 g_b=\frac1{3-b},\qquad z_b=b-1.                                         \tag{19}
\]
All denominators and all three variances are bounded away from zero on \(J\).  Let \(V_b,W_b,Z_b\) be independent centered Gaussian variables with variances \(f_b,g_b,z_b\).  Direct substitution gives
\[
 f_b+g_b=2,
 \qquad3f_b+bg_b=5,
 \qquad9f_b+b^2g_b+z_b=14.                                                \tag{20}
\]
Consequently
\[
 G_b=(V_b+W_b,3V_b+bW_b+Z_b)\sim N(0,\Sigma)                              \tag{21}
\]
for every \(b\in J\).

Independently construct
\[
 L_e=\sum_{j=1}^d j(N_{e,j}-\lambda_{e,j}),
\]
where the independent Poisson rates have a common positive baseline and the jump-\(j\) rate is increased by a fixed \(\eta>0\) only in environment \(e=j\); environments \(e>d\) retain the baseline rates.  Define
\[
 \epsilon_{u,e}=L_e+V_b,\qquad
 \epsilon_{t,e}=W_b,\qquad
 \epsilon_y=Z_b,qquad
 \alpha=1,\quad\beta=b,\quad\gamma=3-b.                                 \tag{22}
\]
Before the perturbation below,
\[
 (T_e,Y_e)=(L_e,3L_e)+G_b,                                                 \tag{23}
\]
so the complete observed law is independent of \(b\).  The latent profiles are \(u_k=\eta(1^k,\ldots,d^k,0,\ldots,0)^\top\), whence the leading calibration block is \(\eta V_d\), \(A=\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf e_1,\ldots,\mathbf e_d\}\), and \(u_k\in A\) for all \(k\).

For an admitted \(r\), let \(\operatorname{He}_r\) be the probabilists' Hermite polynomial and set
\[
 h_r(x)=e^{-x^2}\operatorname{He}_r(\sqrt3x),
 \qquad \mu_r=\frac{r!}{3^{(r+1)/2}}.                                    \tag{24}
\]
Both \(h_r\) and its derivative are bounded.  If \(N\sim N(0,1)\), substitution \(u=\sqrt3x\) followed by the Rodrigues identity and \(r\) integrations by parts gives
\[
 \mathbb E[N^kh_r(N)]
 =3^{-(k+1)/2}\mathbb E[N^k\operatorname{He}_r(N)]
 =\begin{cases}0,&0\leq k<r,\\ \mu_r,&k=r.\end{cases}                   \tag{25}
\]
Every boundary term vanishes because a polynomial times a Gaussian density tends to zero at both endpoints.

Only in environment \(e=d+1\), replace the density of \(W_b\) by
\[
 p_{b,\lambda}(w)=\phi_{g_b}(w)
 \left\{1+\frac{\lambda}{\mu_rg_b^{r/2}}
 h_r\!\left(\frac w{\sqrt{g_b}}\right)\right\}.                         \tag{26}
\]
Compactness of \(J\) and finiteness of the admitted order set give one \(\lambda_0>0\), common to all \(r\), for which the bracket lies in \([1/2,3/2]\) whenever \(0<\lambda\leq\lambda_0\).  Formula (25) at \(k=0,1\) proves normalization and centering.  It shows that raw moments below \(r\) are unchanged and the order-\(r\) raw moment increases by exactly \(\lambda\).  Since the order-\(r\) cumulant is the order-\(r\) moment plus a polynomial in lower moments, its increase is also \(\lambda\).  Gaussian domination gives every absolute moment and the required fixed moment envelope.

Because \(r\geq d+2\), the perturbation leaves \(C\) unchanged.  Lower projected contrasts vanish and
\[
 Q_Ac_r=\lambda\mathbf e_{d+1},
 \qquad Q_Am_r=b\lambda\mathbf e_{d+1}.                                  \tag{27}
\]
Choose fixed coefficient bounds containing \(\alpha=1\), \(b\in J\), and \(\gamma=3-b\), choose \(B>23/10\), choose \(\kappa_0<\eta\sigma_d(V_d)\), and choose the moment envelope above the compact supremum over \(b\in J\), \(0\leq\lambda\leq\lambda_0\), and the finite order set.  All ambient assumptions then hold with constants common to \(r\), and (27) puts each law in \(\mathcal M_r(\lambda)\).

We bound divergence for the complete observations.  Under (21), Gaussian completion of squares gives
\[
 \mathbb E_b[W_b\mid G_b=x]=\ell_b^\top x,
 \qquad \ell_b^\top=g_b(1,b)\Sigma^{-1},                                 \tag{28}
\]
and
\[
 \tau_b^2=\operatorname{Var}_b(W_b\mid G_b)
 =g_b-g_b^2(1,b)\Sigma^{-1}(1,b)^\top
 =-\frac{(b-1)(2b-5)}{3(b-3)^2}>0.                                       \tag{29}
\]
The last quantity is uniformly positive on \(J\).  Conditioning the likelihood ratio in (26) on \(G_b=x\) gives observed density
\[
 \phi_\Sigma(x)\{1+\lambda R_b(x)\},
 \quad
 R_b(x)=\frac1{\mu_rg_b^{r/2}}
 \mathbb E\left[h_r\!\left(
 \frac{\ell_b^\top x+\tau_bN}{\sqrt{g_b}}\right)\right].               \tag{30}
\]
The coefficients in (28)--(30) are continuously differentiable on \(J\), and \(g_b,\tau_b\) are bounded away from zero.  Boundedness of \(h_r,h_r'\) permits differentiation under the Gaussian expectation with envelope \(K(1+\|x\|_2+|N|)\).  Uniformly over the finite order set,
\[
 |R_b(x)|\leq K_4,
 \qquad |\partial_bR_b(x)|\leq K_5(1+\|x\|_2).                           \tag{31}
\]
The mean-value theorem and the finite second moment of \(N(0,\Sigma)\) imply
\[
 \int\{R_b(x)-R_{b'}(x)\}^2\phi_\Sigma(x)\,dx
 \leq K_6|b-b'|^2.                                                        \tag{32}
\]
After reducing \(\lambda_0\) so that \(\lambda_0K_4\leq1/2\), substitution of the two densities into chi-square divergence yields
\[
 \chi^2(P^G_{b,\lambda},P^G_{b',\lambda})
 \leq2K_6\lambda^2|b-b'|^2.                                              \tag{33}
\]
Adding the independent \(L_e\) and applying the common measurable map (23) cannot increase chi-square divergence: the image likelihood ratio is the conditional expectation of the original likelihood ratio, and conditional Jensen's inequality applies to its squared centered value.  Other environments have laws independent of \(b\).  Independence across observations and \(1+x\leq e^x\) therefore give
\[
 1+\chi^2(P_{b,\lambda}^{,n},P_{b',\lambda}^{,n})
 \leq\exp\{K_7n\lambda^2|b-b'|^2\}.                                    \tag{34}
\]
For dominated laws, Cauchy--Schwarz gives
\[
 \|P-Q\|_{\mathrm{TV}}
 \leq\frac12\sqrt{\chi^2(P,Q)}.                                        \tag{35}
\]

Fix \(b_0=2\), let
\[
 h_n=c\min\left\{B,\frac1{\sqrt n\lambda}\right\},
 \qquad b_1=b_0+h_n,                                                       \tag{36}
\]
and choose fixed \(c>0\) small enough that \(b_1\in J\) and (34)--(35) imply
\[
 \|P_{b_0,\lambda}^{,n}-P_{b_1,\lambda}^{,n}\|_{\mathrm{TV}}
 \leq v<\min\{1/2,1-2\alpha_0\}.                                       \tag{37}
\]
For any estimator, let \(D\) be the event that it is closer to \(b_0\) than to \(b_1\).  Its squared error is at least \(h_n^2/4\) under the first law on \(D^c\) and under the second law on \(D\).  The definition of total variation gives
\[
 \max_{j=0,1}\mathbb E_{b_j,\lambda}
 (\widetilde\beta-b_j)^2\geq\frac{h_n^2}{8}(1-v).                        \tag{38}
\]
If a random interval covers both parameters with probability at least \(1-\alpha_0\), then under the first law the two coverage events intersect with probability at least \(1-2\alpha_0-v\).  Connectedness forces length at least \(h_n\) there, so
\[
 \mathbb E_{b_0,\lambda}\operatorname{length}(\mathcal I_n)
 \geq h_n(1-2\alpha_0-v).                                                \tag{39}
\]
Both laws lie in the same shell; hence (38)--(39) apply under shell-only honesty.

For signals \(\lambda\in[\lambda_0,\Lambda]\), the same fixed bounded experiment contains a regular parametric subpath: retain a shell member's \(\alpha\), latent sources, and treatment sources, choose a fixed \(q\in(q_0,q_1)\), set \(\gamma=\alpha q\), use an independent centered Gaussian outcome noise with fixed positive variance \(\sigma_y^2\), and vary \(\beta\) over a fixed interior interval.  These changes leave \(C,A,r^\star\), and shell strength unchanged and fit the fixed envelopes chosen with slack.  In the more informative experiment observing \((U,T,Y)\), two effects separated by \(h\) have
\[
 \operatorname{KL}(P_\beta^n,P_{\beta+h}^n)
 =\frac{h^2}{2\sigma_y^2}
   \sum_{e\in\mathcal E}n_e\mathbb E[T_e^2]
 \leq K_8nh^2.                                                           \tag{40}
\]
Marginalization cannot increase relative entropy, by conditional Jensen's inequality for the image likelihood ratio.  Applying data processing to an indicator event attaining total variation and Taylor's theorem for binary relative entropy gives \(\operatorname{KL}(P,Q)\geq2\|P-Q\|_{\mathrm{TV}}^2\).  Taking \(h=c\min\{B,n^{-1/2}\}\) and repeating (38)--(39) gives the lower orders \(\min\{B^2,n^{-1}\}\) and \(\min\{B,n^{-1/2}\}\), which are equivalent, uniformly for \(\lambda\in[\lambda_0,\Lambda]\), to the expressions in (1) and (3).

Taking infima over estimators and over intervals honest on the shell, and combining (38)--(40) with the upper bounds, proves the two minimax orders on this one fixed compatible experiment.  Shell-only honesty is weaker than honesty on \(\Theta\), so the interval lower bound also applies to the latter class.

If \(\sqrt n\lambda_n\to\infty\), (1) proves uniform mean-square and hence uniform probabilistic consistency on every nonempty shell sequence.  Conversely, if this divergence fails, some subsequence has \(\sqrt n\lambda_n\) bounded.  Along a further subsequence with \(\lambda_n\leq\lambda_0\), (36)--(38) bound minimax risk away from zero; if \(\lambda_n\) is instead bounded below, then \(\sqrt n\lambda_n\to\infty\), a contradiction.  Thus no uniformly consistent estimator exists on the bounded subsequence.  This proves the if-and-only-if consistency frontier on the fixed lower-bound experiment.

added_lemmas.statement:
For every triangular array in \(\Theta\), write the observation in environment \(e\) as \(W_{e,i}=(T_{e,i},Y_{e,i})\), put \(C^+=(C^\top C)^{-1}C^\top\), and put \(h_k=m_k-\beta c_k\).  There are centered first-projection arrays \(\psi^C_{e,n}(W_{e,i})\), \(\psi^c_{e,k,n}(W_{e,i})\), and \(\psi^m_{e,k,n}(W_{e,i})\) such that, simultaneously for \(d+2\leq k\leq R_{\max}\),
\[
 \sqrt n\,\widehat Q(\widehat m_k-\beta\widehat c_k)
 =Z_{n,k}+o_{\mathbb P}(1),
 \qquad
 Z_{n,k}=\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{e\in\mathcal E}\sum_{i=1}^{n_e}
 \pi_e^{-1}\zeta_{e,k,n}(W_{e,i}),
\]
uniformly over \(\Theta\), where
\[
 \zeta_{e,k,n}
 =Q_A\bigl(\psi^m_{e,k,n}-\beta\psi^c_{e,k,n}
       -\psi^C_{e,n}C^+h_k\bigr).
\]
The remainder is uniform in probability, and the stacked vector
\(Z_n=(Z_{n,k}:d+2\leq k\leq R_{\max})\) satisfies
\[
 d_{\mathrm{BL}}\!\left(\mathcal L(Z_n),N(0,\Sigma_n)\right)
 \longrightarrow0,
 \qquad
 \Sigma_n=\sum_{e\in\mathcal E}\pi_e^{-1}
 \mathbb E\bigl[\zeta_{e,n}\zeta_{e,n}^{\top}\bigr],
\]
uniformly over \(\Theta\).  This conclusion allows \(\Sigma_n\) to be singular; \(N(0,\Sigma_n)\) is then the Gaussian law supported on \(\operatorname{im}(\Sigma_n)\).  The term \(-Q_A\psi^C_{e,n}C^+h_k\) is the same-sample estimated-\(A\) correction.  No breakout, nonzero projected flag, or lower bound on a projected cumulant is required.
added_lemmas.proof_tex:
Consider an arbitrary triangular array with every row law in \(\Theta\); all bounds below are uniform over that array and hence over \(\Theta\).  The sampling design gives independent observations within and across environments, with \(W_{e,i}=(T_{e,i},Y_{e,i})\) identically distributed according to \(P_e\) within environment \(e\).  Balanced shares give
\[
 n_e=n\pi_e\geq n\underline\pi . \tag{1}
\]
Thus, for all sufficiently large \(n\), every \(n_e\) is at least \(R_{\max}\), and the small-sample fallback in the cumulant-SVD estimator is inactive.

The coefficient assumptions imply
\[
 |\alpha|\leq a_1,
 \qquad |\beta|\leq B,
 \qquad |\gamma|=|\alpha|\,|\gamma/\alpha|\leq a_1q_1. \tag{2}
\]
The structural equations are equivalently
\[
 T_e=\alpha\epsilon_{u,e}+\epsilon_{t,e},
 \qquad
 Y_e=(\beta\alpha+\gamma)\epsilon_{u,e}
       +\beta\epsilon_{t,e}+\epsilon_y. \tag{3}
\]
Put \(s_0=2R_{\max}+\delta\).  For \(s_0>1\), convexity gives
\[
 |x_1+\cdots+x_j|^{s_0}
 \leq j^{s_0-1}\sum_{a=1}^j|x_a|^{s_0}. \tag{4}
\]
Applying (4) to (3), and using (2) and the source moment envelope, produces a finite constant \(K_W\), depending only on the fixed envelopes, such that
\[
 \sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\max_{e\in\mathcal E}
 \mathbb E_\theta\!\left[\|W_{e,1}\|^{2R_{\max}+\delta}\right]
 \leq K_W. \tag{5}
\]
Consequently all population moments and cumulants of \((T_e,Y_e)\) through order \(R_{\max}\) are uniformly bounded.  In particular, for \(2\leq k\leq R_{\max}\), the norms of \(C\), \(c_k\), \(m_k\), and \(h_k=m_k-\beta c_k\) are uniformly bounded.

We next construct the first projections.  For random variables \(X_1,\ldots,X_k\), the moment--cumulant polynomial is
\[
 \kappa_k(X_1,\ldots,X_k)
 =\sum_{\mathcal P\in\Pi_k}
 (|\mathcal P|-1)!(-1)^{|\mathcal P|-1}
 \prod_{D\in\mathcal P}
 \mathbb E\!\left[\prod_{j\in D}X_j\right], \tag{6}
\]
where \(\Pi_k\) is the finite set of partitions of \(\{1,\ldots,k\}\).  If \(\mathcal P\) has \(s\) blocks, average the corresponding block monomials over \(s\) distinct observations and symmetrize.  This is an unbiased symmetric \(U\)-statistic of order \(s\).  Hence each stipulated sample cumulant of order \(k\) is a fixed finite linear combination of symmetric \(U\)-statistics of orders at most \(k\), with kernels of total polynomial degree at most \(k\).

For one order-\(s\) constituent \(U_{n_e,s}(g)\), let \(g_j\) denote its centered canonical projection of order \(j\), and define
\[
 \psi_g(w)=s\{\mathbb E[g(w,W_2,\ldots,W_s)]-\mathbb E g\}.
\]
Successive subtraction of conditional expectations gives the exact Hoeffding decomposition
\[
 U_{n_e,s}(g)-\mathbb E g
 =\frac1{n_e}\sum_{i=1}^{n_e}\psi_g(W_{e,i})
  +\sum_{j=2}^s {s\choose j}U_{n_e,j}(g_j). \tag{7}
\]
Each \(g_j\) is degenerate in every argument.  Two summands indexed by distinct unordered \(j\)-tuples have covariance zero: one can condition on an index appearing in only one tuple, after which degeneracy annihilates the product.  Therefore
\[
 \mathbb E\!\left[U_{n_e,j}(g_j)^2\right]
 ={n_e\choose j}^{-1}\mathbb E[g_j^2]
 \leq K n_e^{-j}. \tag{8}
\]
The last inequality is uniform because the squared kernel has total degree at most \(2R_{\max}\), and its expectation is bounded by (5) and H\"older's inequality.  There are only finitely many orders, partitions, environments, and coordinates.  Thus the sum of all projections of order at least two in (7) is \(O_{L^2}(n_e^{-1})\), uniformly over \(\Theta\).

Apply the deterministic environment-versus-baseline contrast signs to the relevant constituent first projections and stack their coordinates.  This defines \(\psi^C_{e,n}\), \(\psi^c_{e,k,n}\), and \(\psi^m_{e,k,n}\), with
\[
 \mathbb E[\psi^C_{e,n}(W_{e,1})]=0,
 \quad
 \mathbb E[\psi^c_{e,k,n}(W_{e,1})]=0,
 \quad
 \mathbb E[\psi^m_{e,k,n}(W_{e,1})]=0. \tag{9}
\]
Since \(n_e=n\pi_e\), equations (1), (7), and (8) yield, simultaneously for all relevant \(k\),
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \sqrt n(\widehat C-C)
 &=\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{e\in\mathcal E}\sum_{i=1}^{n_e}
     \pi_e^{-1}\psi^C_{e,n}(W_{e,i})+o_{L^2}(1),\\
 \sqrt n(\widehat c_k-c_k)
 &=\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{e\in\mathcal E}\sum_{i=1}^{n_e}
     \pi_e^{-1}\psi^c_{e,k,n}(W_{e,i})+o_{L^2}(1),\\
 \sqrt n(\widehat m_k-m_k)
 &=\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{e\in\mathcal E}\sum_{i=1}^{n_e}
     \pi_e^{-1}\psi^m_{e,k,n}(W_{e,i})+o_{L^2}(1).
 \end{aligned} \tag{10}
\]
Indeed, after root-\(n\) scaling, the \(O_{L^2}(n_e^{-1})\) degenerate remainder is \(O(n^{-1/2})\) by (1).

Set
\[
 \nu=\min\{1,\delta/R_{\max}\}>0.
\]
Every first projection above is a finite sum of polynomials of degree at most \(R_{\max}\) in one observation; its coefficients are lower-order moments and are bounded by (5).  Conditional Jensen's inequality and (5) therefore give
\[
 \sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\max_{e\in\mathcal E}
 \mathbb E_\theta\!\left[
 \|\psi^C_{e,n}\|^{2+\nu}
 +\sum_{k=2}^{R_{\max}}
 \{\|\psi^c_{e,k,n}\|^{2+\nu}
   +\|\psi^m_{e,k,n}\|^{2+\nu}\}
 \right]\leq K, \tag{11}
\]
because \((2+\nu)R_{\max}\leq2R_{\max}+\delta\).

We now linearize the generated projector.  Let \(P_C=CC^+\), where \(C^+=(C^\top C)^{-1}C^\top\), so \(Q_A=I_{E-1}-P_C\).  The calibration gap licenses the inverse and gives
\[
 \|C^+\|_{\mathrm{op}}=\sigma_d(C)^{-1}\leq\kappa_0^{-1}. \tag{12}
\]
If \(\|H\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq\kappa_0/2\), then for every unit \(v\in\mathbb R^d\),
\[
 \|(C+H)v\|_2
 \geq\|Cv\|_2-\|Hv\|_2
 \geq\sigma_d(C)-\|H\|_{\mathrm{op}}
 \geq\kappa_0/2.
\]
Thus \(C+H\) has rank \(d\).  With \(G=C^\top C\) and \(D=C^\top H+H^\top C+H^\top H\), the exact identity
\[
 (G+D)^{-1}=G^{-1}-G^{-1}DG^{-1}
 +G^{-1}DG^{-1}D(G+D)^{-1} \tag{13}
\]
inserted into
\[
 P_{C+H}=(C+H)\{(C+H)^\top(C+H)\}^{-1}(C+H)^\top
\]
gives, after collecting the terms linear in \(H\),
\[
 P_{C+H}-P_C
 =Q_AHC^+ +(Q_AHC^+)^\top+R_C(H),
 \qquad \|R_C(H)\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq K_P\|H\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2. \tag{14}
\]
The constant \(K_P\) is uniform: (12) bounds \(G^{-1}\), the preceding singular-value bound controls \((G+D)^{-1}\), and (5)--(6) bound \(\|C\|_{\mathrm{op}}\).

Take \(H=\widehat C-C\).  Equations (10)--(11) imply \(\|H\|_{\mathrm{op}}=O_{\mathbb P}(n^{-1/2})\) uniformly, so the event used in (14) has probability tending to one uniformly, and its Taylor remainder is \(O_{\mathbb P}(n^{-1})\).  On that event the rank-\(d\) SVD projector is \(P_{\widehat C}\).  Hence
\[
 \widehat Q-Q_A
 =-Q_A(\widehat C-C)C^+
  -\{Q_A(\widehat C-C)C^+\}^\top
  +o_{\mathbb P}(n^{-1/2}) \tag{15}
\]
uniformly over \(\Theta\).

The established cumulant-cancellation lemma gives, for every \(k\geq2\),
\[
 h_k=m_k-\beta c_k=\alpha^{k-1}\gamma u_k\in A=\operatorname{col}(C),
 \qquad Q_Ah_k=0. \tag{16}
\]
This conclusion uses source independence and the latent-profile-plane condition, but no breakout condition.  The transpose term in (15) therefore annihilates \(h_k\):
\[
 \{Q_A(\widehat C-C)C^+\}^\top h_k
 =C^{+\top}(\widehat C-C)^\top Q_Ah_k=0. \tag{17}
\]
Writing \(\widehat h_k=\widehat m_k-\beta\widehat c_k\), equations (10)--(17) imply
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \sqrt n\,\widehat Q\widehat h_k
 &=\sqrt n\,Q_A(\widehat h_k-h_k)
   +\sqrt n(\widehat Q-Q_A)h_k
   +\sqrt n(\widehat Q-Q_A)(\widehat h_k-h_k)\\
 &=\sqrt n\,Q_A\{(\widehat m_k-m_k)
       -\beta(\widehat c_k-c_k)\}
   -\sqrt n\,Q_A(\widehat C-C)C^+h_k
   +o_{\mathbb P}(1).
 \end{aligned} \tag{18}
\]
The last product in the first line is \(O_{\mathbb P}(n^{-1/2})\), uniformly, because both unscaled estimation errors are \(O_{\mathbb P}(n^{-1/2})\), while \(\beta\), \(h_k\), and \(C^+\) are uniformly bounded.  Substituting (10) into (18) gives
\[
 \sqrt n\,\widehat Q(\widehat m_k-\beta\widehat c_k)
 =\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{e\in\mathcal E}\sum_{i=1}^{n_e}
   \pi_e^{-1}\zeta_{e,k,n}(W_{e,i})+o_{\mathbb P}(1), \tag{19}
\]
where
\[
 \zeta_{e,k,n}
 =Q_A\{\psi^m_{e,k,n}-\beta\psi^c_{e,k,n}
          -\psi^C_{e,n}C^+h_k\}. \tag{20}
\]
There are finitely many \(k\), so the remainders are simultaneous.  Equation (20) displays the same-sample estimated-plane correction, including its negative sign.

Stack (20) over \(d+2\leq k\leq R_{\max}\), and call the result \(\zeta_{e,n}\).  Equations (11)--(12) and the uniform bound on \(h_k\) imply
\[
 \sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\max_{e\in\mathcal E}
 \mathbb E_\theta\|\zeta_{e,n}\|^{2+\nu}\leq K. \tag{21}
\]
Index the independent summands in the stacked \(Z_n\) by \(a=(e,i)\), and put
\[
 X_a=n^{-1/2}\pi_e^{-1}\zeta_{e,n}(W_{e,i}),
 \qquad
 L_n=\sum_a\mathbb E\|X_a\|^{2+\nu}.
\]
By (1) and (21),
\[
 L_n
 \leq K n^{-1-\nu/2}\sum_{e\in\mathcal E}n_e\pi_e^{-(2+\nu)}
 =K n^{-\nu/2}\sum_{e\in\mathcal E}\pi_e^{-(1+\nu)}
 \leq K'n^{-\nu/2}. \tag{22}
\]

For each \(a\), let \(G_a\) be an independent centered Gaussian vector with \(\operatorname{Cov}(G_a)=\operatorname{Cov}(X_a)\).  Fixed dimensionality, followed by Lyapunov's inequality, gives
\[
 \mathbb E\|G_a\|^{2+\nu}
 \leq K\{\operatorname{tr}\operatorname{Cov}(X_a)\}^{1+\nu/2}
 =K\{\mathbb E\|X_a\|^2\}^{1+\nu/2}
 \leq K\mathbb E\|X_a\|^{2+\nu}. \tag{23}
\]
Let \(f\) be bounded by one and one-Lipschitz, and let \(f_\varepsilon(x)=\mathbb E[f(x+\varepsilon Z_0)]\), where \(Z_0\) is standard Gaussian in the fixed ambient dimension.  Differentiating the Gaussian convolution gives
\[
 \sup_x\|D^2f_\varepsilon(x)\|\leq K\varepsilon^{-1},
 \qquad
 \sup_x\|D^3f_\varepsilon(x)\|\leq K\varepsilon^{-2}.
\]
Interpolating these two bounds yields
\[
 \|D^2f_\varepsilon(x)-D^2f_\varepsilon(y)\|
 \leq K\varepsilon^{-(1+\nu)}\|x-y\|^\nu. \tag{24}
\]
Indeed, apply \(\min\{A,Bt\}\leq A^{1-\nu}(Bt)^\nu\) to the uniform second-derivative bound and the third-derivative Lipschitz bound.  The integral Taylor remainder then satisfies
\[
 |f_\varepsilon(x+v)-f_\varepsilon(x)-Df_\varepsilon(x)v
   -\tfrac12v^\top D^2f_\varepsilon(x)v|
 \leq K\varepsilon^{-(1+\nu)}\|v\|^{2+\nu}. \tag{25}
\]
Replace the \(X_a\)'s successively by the \(G_a\)'s.  Conditional on all other summands, the constant, linear, and quadratic terms cancel because each pair has the same zero mean and covariance.  Equations (23)--(25) therefore give
\[
 \left|\mathbb Ef_\varepsilon\!\left(\sum_aX_a\right)
       -\mathbb Ef_\varepsilon\!\left(\sum_aG_a\right)\right|
 \leq K\varepsilon^{-(1+\nu)}L_n. \tag{26}
\]
The coupling defining the convolution also gives
\[
 \sup_x|f_\varepsilon(x)-f(x)|
 \leq\varepsilon\mathbb E\|Z_0\|. \tag{27}
\]
Taking the supremum over the bounded-Lipschitz class in (26)--(27),
\[
 d_{\mathrm{BL}}\!\left(\mathcal L\!\left(\sum_aX_a\right),
                         \mathcal L\!\left(\sum_aG_a\right)\right)
 \leq K\{\varepsilon+\varepsilon^{-(1+\nu)}L_n\}. \tag{28}
\]
When \(L_n>0\), choose \(\varepsilon=L_n^{1/(2+\nu)}\); when \(L_n=0\), all summands vanish almost surely and the two laws coincide.  Equations (22) and (28) prove uniform convergence to zero.

Finally, independence, centering, and \(n_e=n\pi_e\) give
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \operatorname{Cov}\!\left(\sum_aG_a\right)
 &=\operatorname{Cov}\!\left(\sum_aX_a\right)\\
 &=\frac1n\sum_{e\in\mathcal E}n_e\pi_e^{-2}
   \mathbb E[\zeta_{e,n}\zeta_{e,n}^\top]\\
 &=\sum_{e\in\mathcal E}\pi_e^{-1}
   \mathbb E[\zeta_{e,n}\zeta_{e,n}^\top]
 =\Sigma_n. \tag{29}
 \end{aligned}
\]
Thus \(\sum_aG_a\sim N(0,\Sigma_n)\), proving the stated bounded-Lipschitz approximation.  No inverse eigenvalue of \(\Sigma_n\), breakout order, projected-flag lower bound, or shell condition appeared.  If \(\Sigma_n\) is singular, the Gaussian sum is supported on \(\operatorname{im}(\Sigma_n)\); if \(\Sigma_n=0\), it is the point mass at zero.
added_lemmas.justification: This lemma supplies the load-bearing ambient-class linearization and explicitly accounts for estimation of the environmental cumulant plane from the same sample.

added_lemmas.statement:
Put
\[
 \nu=\min\{1,\delta/R_{\max}\},
 \qquad
 \varrho_{\mathrm{AR}}=\frac{\nu}{8+4\nu},
\]
and let \(0<\chi<\varrho_{\mathrm{AR}}\) and \(m_n\to\infty\) be deterministic.  The randomized-jitter Gaussian-multiplier set \(\mathcal C_n^{\mathrm{RJ}}\) is implementable from the stratified observations and auxiliary standard normal draws.  Uniformly over every triangular array in the bounded ambient class \(\Theta\),
\[
 \lim_{n\to\infty}
 \sup_{\theta\in\Theta}
 \left|
 \Pr_\theta\{\beta\in\mathcal C_n^{\mathrm{RJ}}\}
 -(1-\alpha_0)
 \right|=0,
\]
where the probability is unconditional over the observations, all Gaussian multipliers, the observed-statistic jitter, and all Monte Carlo jitters.  In particular, the conclusion includes no-breakout parameters.  It allows the same-sample estimated-\(A\) influence covariance \(\Sigma_n\) to be singular, to change rank with \(n\), or to equal zero, and it uses neither a covariance inverse nor a positive-eigenvalue bound.  Since \(\tau_n=n^{-\chi}\to0\), the randomization vanishes on the root-\(n\) projected-moment scale underlying \(\mathcal C_n\); the displayed limit is exact, rather than conservative, null calibration of an Anderson--Rubin inversion.  No expected-length or diameter optimality is asserted for \(\mathcal C_n^{\mathrm{RJ}}\).

There is a precise atomic limitation for deterministic single-threshold calibration.  If a reference statistic has distribution function \(F\), has an atom at a proposed cutoff \(x_0\), and
\[
 F(x_0-)<1-\alpha_0<F(x_0),
\]
then neither the deterministic rule accepting below \(x_0\) nor the deterministic rule accepting at or below \(x_0\) has acceptance probability \(1-\alpha_0\).  This limitation concerns those deterministic single-threshold conventions at an atom; it is not an impossibility claim about every procedure without external randomization.
added_lemmas.proof_tex:
Write \(\mathcal K=\{d+2,\ldots,R_{\max}\}\), and use the block maximum norm from the construction.  Its dimension \(D_{\mathrm{AR}}=(E-1)(R_{\max}-d-1)\) is fixed.  Every constant below depends only on the fixed coefficient, source-moment, share, and calibration-gap envelopes, and not on a particular member of \(\Theta\).

Balanced shares imply \(n_e\geq\underline\pi n\).  Hence every \(n_e\geq R_{\max}\) for all sufficiently large \(n\), so the construction's small-sample fallback is always defined and is eventually inactive.  At the true value \(b=\beta\), the ambient-class generated-projector expansion gives
\[
 H_n(\beta)=Z_n+R_n,
 \qquad
 Z_n=\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{e\in\mathcal E}\sum_{i=1}^{n_e}
 \pi_e^{-1}\zeta_{e,n}(W_{e,i}), \tag{1}
\]
where \(R_n=o_{\mathbb P}(1)\) uniformly over \(\Theta\), and
\[
 \Sigma_n=\sum_{e\in\mathcal E}\pi_e^{-1}
 \mathbb E[\zeta_{e,n}\zeta_{e,n}^{\top}]. \tag{2}
\]
The same expansion constructs every coordinate of \(\zeta_{e,n}\) from cumulant first projections of polynomial degree at most \(R_{\max}\), \(Q_A\), \(C^+\), and bounded population cumulants.  The moment envelope, coefficient bounds, and calibration gap \(\|C^+\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq\kappa_0^{-1}\) therefore imply, for
\[
 \nu=\min\{1,\delta/R_{\max}\}>0,
\]
that
\[
 \sup_{n}\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\max_{e\in\mathcal E}
 \mathbb E_\theta\|\zeta_{e,n}\|^{2+\nu}\leq K. \tag{3}
\]
The division by \(\sigma_d(C)\) is licensed by \(\sigma_d(C)\geq\kappa_0>0\), and the moment order is sufficient because \((2+\nu)R_{\max}\leq2R_{\max}+\delta\).

First quantify the Gaussian approximation without dividing by an eigenvalue.  Put
\[
 X_{e,i,n}=n^{-1/2}\pi_e^{-1}\zeta_{e,n}(W_{e,i}).
\]
Balanced shares and (3) give
\[
 \sum_{e\in\mathcal E}\sum_{i=1}^{n_e}
 \mathbb E\|X_{e,i,n}\|^{2+\nu}
 \leq K n^{-\nu/2}. \tag{4}
\]
For a function \(f\) bounded by one and one-Lipschitz, let \(f_s\) be its convolution with \(N(0,s^2I_{D_{\mathrm{AR}}})\).  Translation coupling and differentiation of the Gaussian density give
\[
 \|f_s-f\|_\infty\leq Ks,
 \qquad [D^2f_s]_\nu\leq Ks^{-1-\nu}. \tag{5}
\]
Replace the independent summands \(X_{e,i,n}\), one at a time, by independent centered Gaussian vectors having the same covariances.  Taylor's formula through order two cancels the mean and covariance terms.  Its integral remainder and (5) bound the error by \(Ks^{-1-\nu}\) times the sum of the \((2+\nu)\)-moments of the original and Gaussian summands.  If \(G\) is a matching Gaussian summand, fixed dimensionality and Lyapunov's inequality give
\[
 \mathbb E\|G\|^{2+\nu}
 \leq K\{\mathbb E\|X_{e,i,n}\|^2\}^{1+\nu/2}
 \leq K\mathbb E\|X_{e,i,n}\|^{2+\nu}.
\]
Thus (4) yields
\[
 d_{\mathrm{BL}}\bigl(\mathcal L(Z_n),N(0,\Sigma_n)\bigr)
 \leq K\{s+n^{-\nu/2}s^{-1-\nu}\}.
\]
Taking \(s=n^{-\nu/(4+2\nu)}\),
\[
 \sup_{\theta\in\Theta}
 d_{\mathrm{BL}}\bigl(\mathcal L_\theta(Z_n),N(0,\Sigma_n)\bigr)
 \leq K n^{-\nu/(4+2\nu)}. \tag{6}
\]
No step requires \(\Sigma_n\) to be nonsingular.

We also need a rate for the remainder in (1).  For a canonical Hoeffding projection of order \(j\geq2\), the degeneracy argument gives variance \(O(n_e^{-j})\) before root-\(n\) scaling, and therefore at most \(O(n^{-1})\) afterward.  The projector expansion remainder is bounded by \(K\sqrt n\|\widehat C-C\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2\) on \(\{\|\widehat C-C\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq\kappa_0/2\}\).  The first-projection variance calculation gives
\[
 \sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\mathbb E_\theta\|\widehat C-C\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2
 \leq K/n,
 \qquad
 \sup_{\theta\in\Theta}
 \Pr_\theta\{\|\widehat C-C\|_{\mathrm{op}}>\kappa_0/2\}
 \leq K/n. \tag{7}
\]
Consequently,
\[
 \sup_{\theta\in\Theta}
 \mathbb E_\theta\!\left[1\wedge
 \{\sqrt n\|\widehat C-C\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2\}\right]
 \leq Kn^{-1/2}.
\]
Products of two first-order estimation errors have the same truncated-mean order by Cauchy--Schwarz and their \(O(n^{-1})\) mean-square bounds.  Combining these facts with the canonical-projection remainder and the exceptional probability in (7),
\[
 \sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\mathbb E_\theta[1\wedge\|R_n\|]
 \leq Kn^{-1/2}. \tag{8}
\]
Since a bounded one-Lipschitz function changes by at most \(1\wedge\|R_n\|\), equations (6)--(8), together with \(\nu\leq1\), imply
\[
 \sup_{\theta\in\Theta}d_{\mathrm{BL}}
 \bigl(\mathcal L_\theta(H_n(\beta)),N(0,\Sigma_n)\bigr)
 \leq K n^{-\nu/(4+2\nu)}. \tag{9}
\]

We next obtain the quantitative estimated-influence replacement bound.  For an order-\(s\) constituent kernel \(g\), define its population first projection by
\[
 \psi_{g,e}(w)=s\{\mathbb E[g(w,W_2,\ldots,W_s)]-\mathbb E g\}.
\]
If \(s\geq2\), then, conditionally on \(W_{e,i}\), the first average in \(\widehat\psi_{g,e,i}\) is an order-\((s-1)\) \(U\)-statistic based on the remaining observations.  After subtracting its conditional expectation, the number of pairs of summands with overlapping index sets is \(O(n_e^{2s-3})\), whereas the denominator has order \(n_e^{2s-2}\).  The kernel's second moment is uniformly bounded, so the integrated conditional variance is at most \(K/n_e\).  For \(s=1\), the first average is exactly \(g(W_{e,i})\) and has no conditional-estimation error.  For every \(s\), the centering statistic satisfies \(\mathbb E|U_{e,s}(g)-\mathbb E g|^2\leq K/n_e\) by the same overlap count.  Thus, after stacking the finitely many kernels and contrast signs,
\[
 \sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\mathbb E_\theta R_n^\psi\leq K/n,
 \qquad
 R_n^\psi=\frac1n\sum_{e\in\mathcal E}\sum_{i=1}^{n_e}\pi_e^{-2}
 \|\widehat\psi_{e,i}-\psi_{e,n}(W_{e,i})\|^2. \tag{10}
\]
Jensen's inequality for the leave-one-out averages and the \(U\)-statistics, together with \((2+\nu)R_{\max}\leq2R_{\max}+\delta\), also gives uniform \((2+\nu)\)-moment bounds for both \(\widehat\psi_{e,i}\) and \(\psi_{e,n}(W_{e,i})\).

Put \(h_k=m_k-\beta c_k\), \(\widehat h_k=\widehat m_k-\beta\widehat c_k\), and define
\[
 \mathfrak e_n^2
 =\|\widehat Q-Q_A\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2
 +\|\widehat C^\dagger-C^+\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2
 +\sum_{k\in\mathcal K}\|\widehat h_k-h_k\|_2^2.
\]
On \(\{\|\widehat C-C\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq\kappa_0/2\}\), the inverse identity used in the projector expansion gives
\(\|\widehat C^\dagger-C^+\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq K\|\widehat C-C\|_{\mathrm{op}}\).  Off this event, the threshold in the construction gives \(\|\widehat C^\dagger\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq2/\kappa_0\), while \(\|C^+\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq1/\kappa_0\); equation (7) controls the event.  The projector perturbation bound and the \(U\)-statistic mean-square bounds therefore yield
\[
 \sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\mathbb E_\theta\mathfrak e_n^2\leq K/n,
 \qquad
 \sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\mathbb E_\theta\mathfrak e_n\leq Kn^{-1/2}. \tag{11}
\]
Let
\[
 \mathfrak y_n=1+\frac1n\sum_{e\in\mathcal E}\sum_{i=1}^{n_e}\pi_e^{-2}
 \left\{\|\psi_{e,n}(W_{e,i})\|^2+
 \|\widehat\psi_{e,i}\|^2\right\},
 \qquad a=\nu/2.
\]
Convexity of \(x\mapsto x^{1+a}\), the moment bounds following (10), and balanced shares imply
\[
 \sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\mathbb E_\theta\mathfrak y_n^{1+a}\leq K. \tag{12}
\]
Expand the definitions of \(\widehat\zeta_{e,i}(\beta)\) and \(\zeta_{e,n}(W_{e,i})\), adding and subtracting one estimated factor at a time.  The bounds on \(C^+\), \(\widehat C^\dagger\), and \(h_k\) then give the deterministic inequality
\[
 B_n^\zeta:=\frac1n\sum_{e\in\mathcal E}\sum_{i=1}^{n_e}\pi_e^{-2}
 \|\widehat\zeta_{e,i}(\beta)-\zeta_{e,n}(W_{e,i})\|^2
 \leq K\{R_n^\psi+\mathfrak e_n^2\mathfrak y_n\}. \tag{13}
\]
No independence between \(\mathfrak e_n\) and \(\mathfrak y_n\) is used.

Define
\[
 \widetilde\Sigma_n=\frac1n\sum_{e\in\mathcal E}\sum_{i=1}^{n_e}\pi_e^{-2}
 \zeta_{e,n}(W_{e,i})\zeta_{e,n}(W_{e,i})^\top
\]
and
\[
 \widehat\Sigma_n(\beta)=\frac1n\sum_{e\in\mathcal E}\sum_{i=1}^{n_e}\pi_e^{-2}
 \widehat\zeta_{e,i}(\beta)\widehat\zeta_{e,i}(\beta)^\top.
\]
Applying Cauchy--Schwarz to the empirical sums and using (12)--(13) gives
\[
 \|\widehat\Sigma_n(\beta)-\widetilde\Sigma_n\|_{\mathrm{op}}
 \leq K\{(R_n^\psi\mathfrak y_n)^{1/2}
 +\mathfrak e_n\mathfrak y_n+R_n^\psi
 +\mathfrak e_n^2\mathfrak y_n\}. \tag{14}
\]
We integrate this bound rather than relying on convergence in probability.  For each \(t>0\), equations (10) and (12) imply
\[
 \mathbb E[1\wedge R_n^\psi\mathfrak y_n]
 \leq t\mathbb E R_n^\psi+\Pr(\mathfrak y_n>t)
 \leq K\{t/n+t^{-(1+a)}\}.
\]
Choosing \(t=n^{1/(2+a)}\), followed by Jensen's inequality, gives
\[
 \mathbb E[1\wedge(R_n^\psi\mathfrak y_n)^{1/2}]
 \leq Kn^{-\kappa},
 \qquad
 \kappa=\frac{1+a}{2(2+a)}. \tag{15}
\]
Similarly, (11)--(12), without an independence assumption, give
\[
 \mathbb E[1\wedge\mathfrak e_n\mathfrak y_n]
 \leq t\mathbb E\mathfrak e_n+\Pr(\mathfrak y_n>t)
 \leq K\{tn^{-1/2}+t^{-(1+a)}\}.
\]
Taking \(t=n^{1/\{2(2+a)\}}\) gives the same \(Kn^{-\kappa}\) bound.  The two remaining terms in (14) are faster; in particular, splitting on \(\{\mathfrak y_n\leq t\}\) and taking \(t=n^{1/(2+a)}\) gives
\[
 \mathbb E[1\wedge\mathfrak e_n^2\mathfrak y_n]
 \leq Kn^{-(1+a)/(2+a)}.
\]
Consequently,
\[
 \sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\mathbb E_\theta\!\left[
 1\wedge\|\widehat\Sigma_n(\beta)-\widetilde\Sigma_n\|_{\mathrm{op}}
 \right]
 \leq Kn^{-\kappa}. \tag{16}
\]
This is the required uniform-integrability upgrade; the mean-square leave-one-out bound alone would not imply it.

For the empirical covariance of the true influences, each matrix \(\zeta_{e,n}\zeta_{e,n}^\top\) has a uniformly bounded \((1+a)\)-moment by (3).  Truncate its norm at
\[
 \ell_n=n^{1/\{2(1+a)\}}.
\]
The tail expectation is at most \(K\ell_n^{-a}\).  The mean absolute deviation of the average of the centered truncated matrices is bounded by its root mean square, which is at most
\[
 Kn^{-1/2}\ell_n^{(1-a)/2}.
\]
This term is no larger in order than the tail term for \(0<a\leq1/2\).  Since stratified independence and \(n_e=n\pi_e\) give \(\mathbb E\widetilde\Sigma_n=\Sigma_n\),
\[
 \sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\mathbb E_\theta
 \|\widetilde\Sigma_n-\Sigma_n\|_{\mathrm{op}}
 \leq Kn^{-a/\{2(1+a)\}}
 =Kn^{-\nu/(4+2\nu)}. \tag{17}
\]
The chosen exponent satisfies
\[
 2\varrho_{\mathrm{AR}}=\frac{a}{2(1+a)},
 \qquad
 \kappa-2\varrho_{\mathrm{AR}}
 =\frac{1}{2(2+a)(1+a)}>0.
\]
Because \(\tau_n=n^{-\chi}\) with \(\chi<\varrho_{\mathrm{AR}}\), equations (16)--(17) imply
\[
 \sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\mathbb E_\theta\!\left[
 1\wedge\|\widehat\Sigma_n(\beta)-\widetilde\Sigma_n\|_{\mathrm{op}}
 \right]=o(\tau_n^2), \tag{18}
\]
and, by the triangle inequality,
\[
 \sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\mathbb E_\theta\!\left[
 1\wedge\|\widehat\Sigma_n(\beta)-\Sigma_n\|_{\mathrm{op}}
 \right]
 \leq Kn^{-2\varrho_{\mathrm{AR}}}=o(\tau_n^2). \tag{19}
\]

Conditionally on the data, \(G_n^{*(j)}(\beta)\) is exactly Gaussian with covariance \(\widehat\Sigma_n(\beta)\).  For positive semidefinite matrices \(S,T\), the square-root integral
\[
 S^{1/2}=\frac1\pi\int_0^\infty
 t^{-1/2}S(S+tI)^{-1}\,dt
\]
and the resolvent identity, with the integral split at \(t=\|S-T\|_{\mathrm{op}}\), give
\[
 \|S^{1/2}-T^{1/2}\|_{\mathrm{op}}
 \leq K\|S-T\|_{\mathrm{op}}^{1/2}. \tag{20}
\]
This derivation remains valid when either matrix has zero eigenvalues.  Couple the conditional multiplier Gaussian and \(N(0,\Sigma_n)\) as \(\widehat\Sigma_n(\beta)^{1/2}Z\) and \(\Sigma_n^{1/2}Z\), with \(Z\sim N(0,I_{D_{\mathrm{AR}}})\).  Equation (20), fixed-dimensional Gaussian moments, Jensen's inequality, and (19) yield
\[
 \sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\mathbb E_\theta
 d_{\mathrm{BL}}\bigl(
 \mathcal L^*(G_n^{*(j)}(\beta)),N(0,\Sigma_n)
 \bigr)
 \leq Kn^{-\varrho_{\mathrm{AR}}}. \tag{21}
\]

It remains to eliminate atomic discontinuities.  Let \(G_n\sim N(0,\Sigma_n)\), let \(\xi\sim N(0,1)\) be independent, and define
\[
 F_{n,\theta}^{\circ}(t)
 =\Pr\{\|G_n\|_{\max}+\tau_n\xi\leq t\}.
\]
For each \(t\), the map
\[
 x\longmapsto
 \Phi\!\left(\frac{t-\|x\|_{\max}}{\tau_n}\right)
\]
is bounded by one and has Lipschitz constant at most \((\sqrt{2\pi}\tau_n)^{-1}\).  Thus (9), (21), and \(\chi<\varrho_{\mathrm{AR}}\) imply
\[
 \sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\sup_{t\in\mathbb R}
 \left|\Pr_\theta\{V_n(\beta)\leq t\}
 -F_{n,\theta}^{\circ}(t)\right|
 \leq K n^{\chi-2\varrho_{\mathrm{AR}}}=o(1), \tag{22}
\]
and
\[
 \sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\mathbb E_\theta\sup_{t\in\mathbb R}
 \left|\Pr^*\{V_n^{*(j)}(\beta)\leq t\}
 -F_{n,\theta}^{\circ}(t)\right|
 \leq K n^{\chi-\varrho_{\mathrm{AR}}}=o(1). \tag{23}
\]
The ideal distribution is continuous and strictly increasing even when \(\Sigma_n\) is singular or zero, because it has the everywhere-positive density
\[
 t\longmapsto
 \mathbb E\left[
 \tau_n^{-1}\phi\!\left(
 \frac{t-\|G_n\|_{\max}}{\tau_n}
 \right)
 \right]. \tag{24}
\]

Let \(U_n=1-F_{n,\theta}^{\circ}(V_n(\beta))\).  Since \(F_{n,\theta}^{\circ}\) is continuous and strictly increasing, the probability integral transform is exactly uniform when \(V_n(\beta)\) itself has distribution function \(F_{n,\theta}^{\circ}\).  Equation (22) and the elementary inverse-distribution inequalities therefore give
\[
 \sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\sup_{u\in[0,1]}
 |\Pr_\theta(U_n\leq u)-u|\longrightarrow0. \tag{25}
\]
Write
\[
 p_n^*(\beta)=\Pr^*\{V_n^{*(j)}(\beta)\geq V_n(\beta)\}.
\]
The Gaussian jitter makes the conditional comparison distribution continuous, so the weak inequality has no tie term.  Equation (23) gives
\[
 |p_n^*(\beta)-U_n|
 \leq\sup_{t\in\mathbb R}
 \left|\Pr^*\{V_n^{*(j)}(\beta)\leq t\}
 -F_{n,\theta}^{\circ}(t)\right|=o_{\mathbb P}(1) \tag{26}
\]
uniformly over \(\Theta\).  Equations (25)--(26) show that \(p_n^*(\beta)\) converges in distribution to the uniform law on \((0,1)\), uniformly over the full ambient class.  This reasoning does not require a breakout and remains valid at \(\Sigma_n=0\).

Conditionally on the data and \(\xi_0\), the \(m_n\) indicators defining \(\widehat p_{n,m_n}(\beta)\) are independent Bernoulli variables with success probability \(p_n^*(\beta)\).  Hence
\[
 \operatorname{Var}\!\left(
 \widehat p_{n,m_n}(\beta)\mid\text{data},\xi_0
 \right)
 =\frac{p_n^*(\beta)\{1-p_n^*(\beta)\}}{m_n}
 \leq\frac1{4m_n}. \tag{27}
\]
Chebyshev's inequality and \(m_n\to\infty\) make the Monte Carlo error \(o_{\mathbb P}(1)\), uniformly.  Since \(\alpha_0\in(0,1/2)\) is a continuity point of the uniform law,
\[
 \sup_{\theta\in\Theta}
 \left|
 \Pr_\theta\{\widehat p_{n,m_n}(\beta)>\alpha_0\}
 -(1-\alpha_0)
 \right|\longrightarrow0. \tag{28}
\]
By construction, the event in (28) is exactly \(\{\beta\in\mathcal C_n^{\mathrm{RJ}}\}\).  Its probability integrates over the observations, all multiplier draws, \(\xi_0\), and every Monte Carlo jitter.  Also, \(\tau_n\xi_j=o_{\mathbb P}(1)\) for each fixed draw on the root-\(n\) projected-moment scale, because \(\tau_n\to0\).  This proves exact unconditional coverage over \(\Theta\), including no-breakout laws, without an inverse covariance or positive-eigenvalue condition.  The argument is solely a coverage calibration argument and supplies no expected-length or diameter optimality for \(\mathcal C_n^{\mathrm{RJ}}\).

Finally, suppose \(F\) has an atom at \(x_0\).  The deterministic strict single-threshold rule accepts with probability \(F(x_0-)\), whereas the deterministic weak rule accepts with probability \(F(x_0)\).  Under
\[
 F(x_0-)<1-\alpha_0<F(x_0),
\]
neither probability equals \(1-\alpha_0\).  Randomized acceptance on the equality event with probability
\[
 \frac{1-\alpha_0-F(x_0-)}{F(x_0)-F(x_0-)}
\]
does attain \(1-\alpha_0\), since the total acceptance probability is then
\[
 F(x_0-)+\{F(x_0)-F(x_0-)\}
 \frac{1-\alpha_0-F(x_0-)}{F(x_0)-F(x_0-)}
 =1-\alpha_0.
\]
This proves exactly the stated limitation for deterministic single-threshold conventions and no wider impossibility claim.
